evidence.text: A hand 扌 holding a weapon 戈
Pictograph of a weapon or farming tool with a forked blade and long handle. The meaning "I; me" is a phonetic loan.
施身自謂也。或說我，頃頓也。从戈从𠄒。𠄒，或說古垂字。一曰古殺字。凡我之屬皆从我。

A pictogram (象形) of a trident-like weapon or tool (note the oracle bone script form 𢦐). Jao & Zeng (1985, pp. 289–290) conjecture about its similarity to a kind of three-bladed polearm found at archaeological sites. Cf. 戈 (“polearm”), which is the same weapon but with a single blade instead of three. It was already borrowed for sound as an instance of jiajie (假借) for the pronoun 我 (OC *ŋaːlʔ, “I”) since the oracle bone script.
Guo Moruo considers it to be the original character for 錡 (OC *ɡral, “a kind of war axe with three blades or teeth”).
Folk etymology considers it to be an ideograph of a hand (手) holding a weapon (戈) to protect oneself.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋa. Cognate with 吾 (OC *ŋaː), Burmese ငါ (nga, “I”), Hakka 𠊎 (ngài). The expected Mandarin pronunciation is ě (now only found in a few Northern dialects); wǒ is "a col[loquial] archaism" (Schuessler, 2007).
Schuessler further decomposes 我 *ŋâiʔ (his reconstruction) into *ŋa + *i, which he terms an "independent suffix" which also appears in some Tibeto-Burman cognates of this pronoun. DeLancey and Benedict believe that the *-i here was an "information structure marker". But given how Sagart believes 我 was originally plural (Sagart 1999:142) and DeLancey discovered that first-person plural compounds of *ŋa (“I”) and *i (“we”) exist in e.g. Raji and Stau, it is also possible that the -iʔ element is actually *i (“we”) fused onto the singular.

Etymological analysis: 會意

Early 我 resembles a long-handled toothed implement, interpreted as a saw or related weapon. It was borrowed as a first-person pronoun. Oracle examples include a plural self-reference; bronze inscriptions also use it for the speaker. Specific identifications of the implement differ.
evidence.title: 我 — historical form and meaning

evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as a toothed, long-handled implement, interpreted as a saw or saw-like ancient weapon. It reports oracle-bone uses for diviner names and a state name as well as a first-person plural pronoun, citing 合集 9688 我受年 (“May we receive a harvest”). It reports bronze use as a first-person pronoun and gives the Mao Gong ding phrase 虔夙夕惠我一人 (“diligently assist me, one person”). Its account also records competing identifications: Guo Moruo linked the implement to 錡 in the Odes; other scholars identify it with a three-toothed axe-like weapon or a multi-ge halberd. These are source interpretations, not settled object identification.
evidence.title: 我 — 漢語多功能字庫, oracle-bone component and form/meaning history

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, National Taiwan University
evidence.text: The article argues that early 我 depicts a toothed, axe-like ritual or ceremonial implement, while noting that no Shang object matching the graph has yet been found. Similar three-toothed weapons are known from Middle Western Zhou contexts, including the 1975 Zhuangbai find, but this does not prove that the depicted Shang-era object was identical. It records Guo Moruo and Lin Yun’s proposed identification with 錡, while a different proposal associates 我 with a ring-shaped jade or stone axe form; the article questions the latter fit. It also argues that 義 and 羲 preserve the weapon sense, an interpretation presented as indirect corroboration rather than proof.
evidence.title: 戚戚我心 – 古漢字的「戚」與「我」

evidence.source: 說文解字在線 (Shuowen.org), quoting 說文 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The Shuowen entry defines 我 as “施身自謂也” (a self-designation), records an alternative explanation “頃頓也,” and analyzes the seal form as 从戈从𠄒, with alternative interpretations of 𠄒 and a note that it may be an ancient graph for 殺. Xu Kai’s later gloss interprets 戈 as a weapon held for self-protection. Duan Yucai cautions that 𠄒 is uncertain and suggests it may be phonetic if it represents 垂; if it represents 殺, that analysis fails. This is a historical lexicographic account, not direct confirmation of the earliest graph’s components.
evidence.title: 說文解字「我」

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry indexes numerous graphic variants for 我, including 𢦐 and 𢦠, and identifies its transmitted Shuowen record under 我部. Many referenced early-script image collections are listed as unavailable in the opened entry, so this page supports variant existence and cataloguing but does not by itself establish a detailed dated evolution sequence.
evidence.title: A01473 (我) — Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 教育部重編國語辭典修訂本 resource reproduced by 字源考釋
evidence.text: The consulted entry summarizes the graph as progressing through oracle-bone, bronze, seal, and standard forms, with the standard form close to seal. It interprets the early graph as a bladed, toothed axe-like weapon and says it was later borrowed for the first-person pronoun. The page gives no dated individual glyph specimens in its accessible text; detailed chronology and claims of specific graphical corruption therefore remain unverified here.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 — 我

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction dataset
evidence.text: The authors’ 2014 Baxter–Sagart dataset documentation describes its table as providing Old Chinese reconstructions alongside Middle Chinese transcription, with Middle Chinese notation representing categories from historical sources rather than a direct phonetic recording. The dataset PDF search result reports 我 as Mandarin wǒ, Middle Chinese ngaX, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *ŋˤajʔ. The PDF could not be opened during this session, so the character-specific transcription was checked in a secondary compilation and the primary dataset access failure is retained in the audit.

These are separate reconstruction systems and should not be merged. These reconstructions concern the pronoun/character reading; they do not independently establish the pronunciation or name of the pictured implement.

evidence.text: The dossier proposes that the first-person pronoun is a phonetic loan and supplies competing Old Chinese reconstructions for 我. The consulted sources support early use of the whole graph for the pronoun and the separate hypothesis that the graph depicts a tool or weapon, but they do not independently recover the depicted implement’s spoken name or show that its name matched the pronoun. Thus the likely borrowing is a whole-graph loan; no part of the graph is established here as a phonetic component, and the object-name sound match remains unproven.

gaps: No direct oracle-bone or bronze inscription facsimile was visually inspected. The CUHK database reports source collections and examples, but individual glyph shapes and readings were not independently checked against plates.

The depicted object is disputed: saw-like implement, toothed axe/weapon, ritual implement, and other proposals appear in the consulted literature. The source word/name and pronunciation of the object are not independently recoverable from the inspected sources.

The pronoun is already attested on oracle bones, including an example interpreted as first-person plural. This establishes early graph use for the pronoun, not the exact date or process of borrowing. Historical scholars disagree about number scope; CUHK gives a plural reading for 合集 9688 and characterizes it as often plural, while other interpretations exist.

No continuous, individually dated chain of glyph specimens was established here for oracle-bone through bronze, seal, clerical, and regular scripts. A consulted summary asserts those stages, but detailed claims about particular hooks or corruptions need direct paleographic verification.

The Shuowen component analysis is internally uncertain in later commentary: 戈 is explicit in the received analysis, but the identity/function of 𠄒 is unresolved and Shuowen's alternate relation to 殺 does not settle the early graph's shape.

The competing Old Chinese forms *ŋˤajʔ and *ŋaːlʔ belong to different reconstruction systems. The primary Baxter–Sagart dataset failed to open, and the inspected publisher page did not provide its entry for 我.

No evidence was found in the inspected sources that identifies a component within 我 as a phonetic element. The sound-loan account concerns reuse of the whole graph for the pronoun; similarity between the reconstructed pronoun and an assumed weapon name is unverified.

The image candidates are modern vector redrawings. Their source pages cite underlying historical-glyph collections and examples, but this research did not independently inspect the source plates or image pixels. Captions should therefore identify the represented script and cited source specimen without claiming that the SVG is a photograph or an independently verified tracing. The Commons file pages describe reuse rights; preserve their stated credit/permission provenance.

The review correction is supported: the selected implement depiction should not be labeled an earliest-attested sense, because the sources report early pronoun and other uses without establishing relative chronology. The interpretive implement sense is better labeled probable or proposed, with its period tied to early forms rather than asserted as chronologically prior.

The Commons page explicitly calls the redraw Western Zhou bronze-script style, so that label is supported as the file's own caption. However, the cited 兮甲盤 specimen is identified separately, and no independent catalog source establishing its period/script classification was inspected. A cautious record should state 'bronze-script redraw; cited specimen 兮甲盤, 集成10174' and attribute the Western Zhou label to Commons rather than presenting it as independently verified.

No direct inscription plate or artifact image was visually inspected in this research step. The exact object represented by 我, its spoken name, and the sound basis for borrowing the whole graph for the pronoun remain unresolved.
The bronze-script category/style label is directly reported by Commons; this research did not independently verify that label against the original inscription or a specialist paleographic catalogue.

items.selection_reason: Complements the oracle-script candidate with a separately cited bronze-style form, without implying that the two images establish a sequence.
items.rights: Commons reports courtesy and permission under the Richard Sears Agreement and marks the vector representation public domain. Consult the file page for the stated source-credit and permission details.

limitations.text: Early forms are interpreted as toothed, long-handled implements, but proposals differ on whether the object was a saw-like tool, an axe-like weapon, or something else. The depicted object's identity and spoken name remain unresolved, so the proposed sound link to the pronoun cannot be demonstrated.
Both images are modern redrawings. The bronze file is labeled Western Zhou style and cites 兮甲盤, but the cited vessel date does not independently establish this glyph's date, location, or reading.

search_audit.query: Open the Wikimedia Commons file description for 我 oracle script and inspect cited source and reuse terms
search_audit.outcome: Opened and inspected the description page. It identifies the work as a modern redraw, cites the Sinica Database specimen, and states source-image and vector-representation reuse terms.

search_audit.query: Open the Wikimedia Commons file description for 我 bronze script and inspect cited specimen and reuse terms
search_audit.outcome: Opened and inspected the description page. It labels the redraw Western Zhou bronze-script style and cites 兮甲盤, 集成10174. The page’s thumbnail and direct image URLs could not be accessed through the web tool; the provided visual review noted the rendered glyph’s appearance.

search_audit.query: 兮甲盤 date King Xuan fifth year 823 BCE
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the vessel entry, which gives 823 BCE. This dates the vessel only; it does not independently verify the cited glyph’s location or reading.

gaps: The Commons pages document their own source and rights claims, but their cited original plates were not independently inspected in this step. The bronze image preview was inaccessible through the web tool; visual description follows the supplied reviewer’s rendered-image report.

The bronze page’s 兮甲盤 citation and Western Zhou style label do not independently establish that this individual glyph is present at a verified location on the vessel. Keep the vessel date attached to the cited specimen, not presented as a confirmed date for the glyph.
Both candidates are modern vector redrawings, not photographs of ancient artifacts. Their proposed captions do not treat their forms as a proven sequence of graphic change.
